entries.title: Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.
entries.content:
jlongen-aws/blog-assets

Viewer • Updated • 1

Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.

Enterprise Article

Many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.

This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, 

torch.compile
, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:
  • How to configure 
    torch.profiler
    with the Neuron backend and capture a clean trace.
  • How to read the 
    key_averages()
    table to identify which operations consume Neuron device time and compare their Self CPU time.
  • How to follow one operation through Neuron Explorer, from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution on a NeuronCore.
  • How these signals change across three implementations of the same operation.

Neuron as a PyTorch Backend

Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.

The Neuron backend uses PyTorch's 

PrivateUse1
extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as 
cuda
. The 
torch_neuronx
package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating New Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.

Set Up the Profiler

You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:

  • NeuronConfig
    controls which Neuron data streams and NeuronCores to capture and where to write the output. You pass it to 
    torch.profiler.profile
    as 
    experimental_config
    .
  • NeuronProfiler
    takes a 
    NeuronConfig
    and provides an 
    export_trace
    callback. The callback writes the framework trace, 
    trace.json
    , alongside the Neuron system traces.
nc = NeuronConfig(
    modes=[ProfileMode.DEVICE, ProfileMode.RUNTIME],
    profile_output_dir=OUTPUT_DIR,
    capture_enabled_for_nc='0',
    correlate_device_time=True,
)
exporter = NeuronProfiler(nc)

The 

modes
parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The 
capture_enabled_for_nc
parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting 
correlate_device_time=True
propagates device time from the trace into the 
key_averages()
table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available 
ProfileMode
values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.

Tooling: Neuron Explorer

Neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what 

key_averages()
reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.

After profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched 

.neff
and 
.ntff
files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching 
.neff
and 
.ntff
files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.

Profile RMSNorm

For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.

You profile three implementations of the same operation:

  • Naive RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations: multiply, mean, add, reciprocal square root, and multiply.
  • torch.rms_norm()
    , the PyTorch built-in lowered to a single fused Neuron kernel.
  • Naive RMSNorm with 
    torch.compile
    , using the same operations as the first implementation.

The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.

All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the 

torch-neuronx
examples directory.

Profile 1: Naive PyTorch Operations

Start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.

device = torch.device('neuron')

x = torch.randn(4, 512, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device=device)
weight = torch.ones(512, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device=device)

def rms_norm_fn(t):
    x_sq = t * t                                    # square
    mean_sq = x_sq.mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)       # mean of squares
    rms = torch.rsqrt(mean_sq + 1e-6)               # 1 / sqrt(mean_sq + eps)
    return t * rms * weight                         # normalize + scale

Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:

  • Include 
    ProfilerActivity.PrivateUse1
    to collect activity from the Neuron device.
  • Pass 
    NeuronConfig
    as 
    experimental_config
    to enable the Neuron-specific Kineto features.

The schedule uses 

wait=2
, 
warmup=1
, and 
active=1
across four 
prof.step()
calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.

Call 

torch.neuron.synchronize()
inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.
with torch.profiler.profile(
    activities=[ProfilerActivity.CPU, ProfilerActivity.PrivateUse1],
    experimental_config=nc,
    record_shapes=False,
    schedule=torch.profiler.schedule(wait=2, warmup=1, active=1),
) as prof:
    for step in range(4):
        with torch.no_grad():
            _ = rms_norm_fn(x)
        torch.neuron.synchronize()
        prof.step()

After profiling finishes, inspect the 

key_averages()
table. Sort by 
self_privateuse1_time_total
to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full 
key_averages()
output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.
print(prof.key_averages().table(sort_by="self_privateuse1_time_total", row_limit=4))

The key averages table shows that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

The table shows which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. 

aten::mul
has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.
Name# CallsSelf CPUSelf NEURON% NEURON
aten::mul360.9 μs1,164.5 μs49.5%
aten::add126.6 μs434.6 μs18.5%
aten::rsqrt115.6 μs415.0 μs17.6%
aten::mean121.1 μs340.8 μs14.5%

Self NEURON total: 2.355 ms

Each row maps directly to the function. 

aten::mul
runs for 
x * x
, 
x * rms
, and the final multiplication by 
weight
. 
aten::mean
reduces the last dimension. 
aten::add
adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. 
aten::rsqrt
computes the reciprocal square root.

Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.

Read the Trace in Explorer

In Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as 

nrta_execute_schedule
, and device execution in the hardware lane as 
nc_exec_running
.

The system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:

LaneLabel suffixWhat it shows
Framework dispatch
framework/TID:
 Operator dispatch events (PrivateUse1 runtime), grouped by thread ID.
Framework device
framework/Stream:
 Device interaction events (PrivateUse1 driver), grouped by stream number.
Neuron Runtime
neuron_rt/NC:
 Neuron Runtime API calls, grouped by logical NeuronCore.
Neuron Hardware
neuron_hw/NC:
 Hardware execution events, grouped by physical NeuronCore.

In eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow 

aten::mul.Tensor
from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.

The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.

Profile 2: torch.rms_norm

Replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in 

rms_norm
function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:
def rms_norm_fn(t):
    return torch.rms_norm(t, [512], weight)

The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.

Name# CallsSelf CPUSelf NEURON% NEURON
aten::_fused_rms_norm147.6 μs403.3 μs100%

Self NEURON total: 403.3 μs

The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.

Compare the Lowering Path

In the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.

Profile 3: Naive PyTorch with torch.compile

For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with 

torch.compile
.

With 

@torch.compile(backend="neuron")
, TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.
@torch.compile(backend='neuron', fullgraph=True)
def naive_compiled(t):
    x_sq = t * t
    mean_sq = x_sq.mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
    rms = torch.rsqrt(mean_sq + 1e-6)
    return t * rms * weight

The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.

Name# CallsSelf CPUSelf NEURON% NEURON
Torch-Compiled Region: 0/0198.4 μs375.5 μs100%

Self NEURON total: 375.5 μs

The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.

The table shows one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to 

torch.rms_norm
, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

Side-by-Side Summary

VariantNEURON timeSelf CPU timeOperator calls
Naive ops2,355 µs~125 µs6
torch.rms_norm403 µs~48 µs1
Naive + torch.compile376 µs~98 µs1

Both 

torch.rms_norm
and 
torch.compile
fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as 
x_sq
and 
mean_sq
between separately dispatched operations.

Conclusion 

key_averages()
shows which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.

You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or 

torch.compile
can reduce its cost.

In Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

Special thanks to Aritra Roy Gosthipaty for the inspiration to begin this series, and to my peers Pinak Panigrahi, Samir Araujo, Akhil Azhikodan, Esha Lakhotia and the rest for reviewing!

entries.title: Granite Speech 5.0: Transcribe, Translate, and Attribute more Accurately and Faster
entries.content:
ibm-granite/granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus

Automatic Speech Recognition • 2B • Updated • 34.5k • 96

Granite Speech 5.0: Transcribe, Translate, and Attribute more Accurately and Faster

Enterprise Article

We're excited to share three updates to IBM's Granite Speech collection: a new speech-language model, granite-speech-5.0-2b, and revised versions of two models the community already uses, granite-speech-5.0-470m-turboctc and granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus. Together they cover the full range of enterprise speech work: transcription and translation with high accuracy, extremely fast transcription at the edge, and recordings where who spoke, and when, matter as much as what was said.

ModelStatusWhat's newBest for
granite-speech-5.0-2b
 NewMore accurate, noise- and reverb-robust automatic speech recognition (ASR), language-ID prompting, 2,000-term keyword biasing, better long-form translationHigh-accuracy multilingual transcription and translation
granite-speech-5.0-470m-turboctc
 UpdatedMultilingual, native punctuation and capitalization, and more robust to noise and reverbHigh-throughput and on-device transcription
granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus
 UpdatedImproved speaker attribution, timestamps, keyword biasing, and long-speech performanceMeetings, calls, and other multi-speaker recordings

Granite Speech 5.0 2B: more accurate, more robust, more control 

granite-speech-5.0-2b
is the successor to 
granite-speech-4.1-2b
at the same parameter count. It transcribes English, French, German, Spanish, Portuguese, and Japanese, and translates to and from English in those languages, plus English to Italian and Mandarin. It was trained on 390,000 hours of public audio, plus synthetic data built for Japanese ASR, keyword biasing, and translation.

What's new compared with 4.1 2B Speech:

  • More accurate, more robust English ASR: Higher accuracy on English short-form benchmarks, and better handling of noise, reverberation, and distant-microphone speech.
  • Language ID prompting: Name the input language in the prompt to steer multilingual transcription.
  • Better long-form and conversational translation: Translation holds up for longer with more natural speech, not just short read sentences.
  • Keyword lists up to 2,000 terms: Bias transcription and translation toward product names, people, and acronyms, in every supported language.
  • Punctuation and capitalization on request: Ask for formatted output in the prompt; capitalization F1 ranges from 89.7 to 99.5 across our test sets.

The model ships under Apache 2.0 with support in Transformers, vLLM, llama.cpp, and mlx-audio for Apple Silicon.

Chart 1: granite-speech-5.0-2b ranks #2 among top open-weight ASR models on average English WER (5.06%). Lower is better. Results are unofficial, as of 15 October 2026, and averaged over the Open ASR Leaderboard’s public English short-form test sets.

Granite Speech 5.0 Turbo CTC: now multilingual, more robust, and even faster

When we introduced Turbo CTC in August, it was an English-only, 470M-parameter encoder built for speed. This revision keeps that footprint and adds the three things users asked for most:

  • Multilingual transcription: English, Japanese, Spanish, German, French, Italian, and Portuguese.
  • Native punctuation and capitalization: Transcripts come out ready to read, with no separate punctuation or truecasing step.
  • More robust in difficult acoustics: Training that explicitly targets reverberant audio makes Turbo CTC more robust in echoey rooms and far-field recordings.

It's also faster. By compiling a single Conformer block and reusing its graph across the stack, we cut warmup time and pushed Turbo CTC to 19,870 RTFx on the Open ASR Leaderboard, up from roughly 12,600 RTFx at launch: about 1.6x faster, at the same accuracy level.

Chart 2: Average WER vs. RTFx on the Open ASR Leaderboard (English short-form, 9 public test sets, as of October 2026). Lower WER and higher RTFx are better; RTFx is on a log scale.

Granite Speech 4.1 2B Plus: better at who said what, and when

The updated 

granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus
is tuned for the recordings enterprises actually have: meetings, support calls, and interviews with several speakers running long. It keeps the 4.1 name because the architecture, prompt format, and API are unchanged, so it's a drop-in replacement for the current model with improved weights. This revision improves four areas:
  • Speaker attribution: More accurate labeling of who is speaking. Word diarization error rate (WDER) drops 7%, and speaker-attributed WER (cpWER) drops 7% overall.
  • Timestamps: Average timestamp shift (AAS) is cut by more than half, yielding tighter timing in captions, search, and review.
  • Long-speech performance: WER on long-form test sets drops 24%.
  • Keyword biasing: Errors on biased keywords fall 45% with 20-term keyword lists.

Timestamps, short speechAAS (average timestamp shift)29.2726.20

Speaker attributionWDER4.404.10

Get started

Not sure which model to pick? Start here:

  • Need high transcription accuracy, translation, or keyword biasing? Use granite-speech-5.0-2b.
  • Need raw speed or on-device transcription? Use granite-speech-5.0-470m-turboctc, and try it in the browser with our WebGPU streaming demo.
  • Working with meetings or multi-speaker calls? Use granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus.

These models are all released under an Apache 2.0 license with native support in Transformers. Full evaluation results, architecture details, training data, and usage examples are on each model card. We recommend pairing them with Granite Guardian for production deployments that need additional risk detection.

Give them a try and let us know what you think!

entries.title: NVIDIA Kumo Forecast Combines Pretrained Time-Series Representations with Historical Pattern Retrieval and Interpretability
entries.content:
nvidia/Kumo-Forecast

Updated • 16

NVIDIA Kumo Forecast Combines Pretrained Time-Series Representations with Historical Pattern Retrieval and Interpretability

Enterprise + Article

Highlights (TL;DR)

NVIDIA Kumo Forecast (formerly known as NV-Tesseract Forecasting) is a multi-variate time-series forecasting model that combines a pretrained Transformer backbone with Domain-Aware Representation and Retrieval (DARR), a context-enhanced forecasting mode that blends direct model predictions with patterns retrieved from historical data. This includes interpretability of the results. Built on the MOMENT-1-large backbone, Kumo Forecast uses an approximately 340-million-parameter base encoder plus a trainable forecasting head.

The library provides a DataFrame-first API, configurable forecast horizons, optional historical context for retrieval, and an interpretability framework that produces horizon-specific explanations without modifying the underlying forecaster.

Kumo-Forecast is available under Apache 2.0 license.

Model code: NVIDIA/Kumo-TS

Model weights: nvidia/Kumo-Forecast

The Shift to Context-Enhanced Time-Series Forecasting

A forecasting system can draw on two different sources of information: representations learned during pretraining and historical observations available for the current application. Kumo-Forecast brings these together through a pretrained forecasting model and an optional retrieval pathway over historical context.

In its direct forecasting path, Kumo-Forecast uses a MOMENT-based Transformer and a trained forecasting head to predict future values. In Domain Aware Representation and Retrieval (DARR) mode, it also retrieves related patterns from historical data using a nearest-neighbor approach and combines that information with the direct forecast.

This creates a distinction between the model’s input window and its retrieval context. The input window supplies recent observations for the forecast; a separate historical DataFrame can supply additional context for pattern retrieval. Developers can adjust how strongly the final prediction relies on each pathway through the library’s configuration options.

Further information on DARR mode can be found in this published paper, Memory-Augmented Forecasting: Scalability and Generalization Across Temporal Domains

How Kumo Forecast Works

Kumo-Forecast combines four main components: a pretrained temporal encoder, a trainable forecasting head, historical-pattern retrieval mechanism and an interpretability framework.

Pretrained Temporal Representations: The model uses the MOMENT-1-large Transformer encoder as its backbone. The architecture keeps encoder and embedder weights frozen while training the forecasting head, separating the pretrained representation model from the task-specific prediction layer.

Direct Forecasting: The forecasting head maps the model’s representations to future values for the requested horizon. For horizons beyond the model’s native capability, there is support for autoregressive extension. This distinguishes a directly generated forecast from a longer forecast that extends predictions recursively.

Domain-Aware Representation and Retrieval: DARR augments direct forecasting with k-nearest-neighbor retrieval from historical context data. This process combines direct forecasts with historical-pattern retrieval, while the SDK accepts the historical context through a separate context_df argument.

Interpretability: Kumo-Forecasting also includes a model-agnostic interpretability framework. When enabled, it produces an explanation bundle containing lag and feature attributions per forecast horizon, semantic-flow diagnostics, trajectory-stability diagnostics, and optional embedding Integrated Gradients.These outputs accompany the forecast rather than requiring a different forecasting architecture.

Further details on interpretability can be found in this paper, NVExplain: Explaining Time Series Forecasting with Latent Trajectory Analysis and Structure-Preserving Surrogates

Limitations

Data must be numeric, temporal data. Supported input sequence lengths include 256, 512, 1024, and 2048 observations. Inputs consist of a timestamp column and one or more numeric value columns, represented as a pandas DataFrame or a CSV/JSON input. When leveraging DARR mode, the dimensions of the context must be similar to the context of the input.

Demo: Predictive Maintenance

The Factory Operations (FOX) Blueprint includes Early Access to the Predictive Maintenance module which leverages Kumo Anomaly and Kumo Forecast. It analyzes real-time data to predict future anomalies.

Demo: Platform Integration

Please click on the image below to access the session from GTC San Jose 2026

Start Building with Kumo Forecast

For an application-specific evaluation, compare the direct and retrieval-enhanced configurations on the same held-out forecasting windows. Validate forecast quality across the intended horizons and operating conditions, consistent with NVIDIA’s requirement for use-case-specific testing

Model code: NVIDIA/Kumo-TS

Model weights: nvidia/Kumo-Forecast

The Kumo-TS repository additionally provides an example for fine-tuning Kumo-Forecast on a user-supplied CSV. Developers therefore have both a pretrained inference workflow and a documented starting point for adapting the model to their own data.

entries.title: FairStress: A deeper evaluation of fairness in LLM decision-making
entries.content:
allenai/fairstress

Updated • 55 • 4

FairStress: A deeper evaluation of fairness in LLM decision-making

Enterprise Article

📄 Tech Report | 🤗 Data | 💻 Code

Today we’re introducing FairStress, a benchmark for measuring demographic fairness in LLMs beyond the choice a model ultimately makes in decisions impacting people. FairStress is available for download, and we’re also building it into Olmo-eval, our open workbench for running and comparing model evaluations.

Models are increasingly being used in high-stakes settings where their outputs can affect people’s opportunities, resources, and care, from screening job applicants and approving loans to prioritizing patients for treatment and evaluating students for admissions. Standard demographic fairness benchmarks often test whether a model selects the same candidate in otherwise identical scenarios after the candidates’ demographic identities are swapped. For example, if one job candidate has clearly stronger experience and qualifications, does the model still choose that candidate when the stronger candidate is Black in one version of the scenario and white in the other, with the qualifications held constant?

Arriving at the same answer in two versions of a scenario can hide meaningful differences in how readily a model changes that decision when challenged, however. Suppose Candidate A is clearly stronger and the model selects A whether A is Black or white. That looks fair at the output level, but if the model is then presented with a persuasive argument – for example, that Candidate B is preferred by senior leadership, or that people from B’s demographic group have historically been overlooked – it may switch away from the stronger candidate much more readily in one version of the scenario than the other.

FairStress is designed to measure these hidden asymmetries.

Across open-weight and frontier models including Olmo, Llama, Qwen, Gemma, Claude, and the GPT family, and across multiple stages of training, we find that the same persuasive arguments – which we call adversarial prefixes – can make models more or less likely to change their decisions depending on which demographic group the argument favors. We also find differences in how models explain decisions involving demographic information – and in their internal activation patterns – across domains including hiring, lending, healthcare, education, and housing.

With FairStress, our target is symmetric fairness—when the evidence supports a decision, a model should apply the same criteria and be equally resistant to changing that decision regardless of which demographic group benefits. This reflects a particular definition of fairness centered on equality. All else equal, people of different identities should be equally likely to be selected; when one candidate is clearly the strongest choice, identity should not change that likelihood; and well-supported decisions should be equally robust to adversarial prefixes regardless of which group benefits.

FairStress does not attempt to capture every conception of fairness. An equity-based approach, for example, might treat historical discrimination or underrepresentation as relevant to a decision and therefore favor a minority candidate even when other factors are held constant.

Measuring fairness beyond the final answer

FairStress contains 300 realistic two-candidate decision scenarios across 29 domains including hiring, healthcare, lending, education, housing, and criminal justice. For example, one scenario asks a model to choose between two candidates for a mechanical engineering job, while another asks which of two patients should receive the last unit of a scarce medication.

Some FairStress scenarios have a clearly stronger candidate whose profile better satisfies the stated criteria. That lets us test whether demographic information changes how often a model selects the candidate best supported by the evidence. Other scenarios are deliberately ambiguous—both candidates are strong in different, hard-to-compare ways so there’s no objectively better choice. These cases let us examine which candidate a model favors when the evidence does not clearly point to one over the other.

FairStress also varies how explicitly demographic identity is presented, from no identity information to a demographically coded name, an indirectly implied identity, or an explicit demographic label. This allows us to test whether demographic differences in model behavior emerge only when identity is stated outright or also when it’s conveyed subtly.

Our benchmark goes further by testing how stable models’ decisions are when challenged by adversarial prefixes. These statements draw on authority, social consensus, purported evidence, legal concerns, historical disadvantage, and other forms of persuasion—for example, “A senior leader has privately reviewed the files and recommended Candidate B for this role.” We then measure whether a model changes its choice in response. Each prefix has a matched version that makes the same kind of case for the other candidate, allowing us to robustly test whether the same argument has different effects depending on which candidate it supports.

Combining these variations in demographic identity and prefix expands FairStress’ 300 scenarios into more than 13 million test cases. Alongside the full benchmark, we’ve developed FairStress-Core, a 50K-item subset selected using item response theory, following our Fluid Benchmarking approach. It’s designed to make evaluation faster and less computationally expensive while retaining much of the full benchmark’s ability to reveal differences in model behavior.

Models do not always hold correct answers equally

In our experiments with FairStress, we found little difference in model behavior when prompts contained no demographic information. When one candidate was clearly stronger, models selected that candidate at nearly the same rate across otherwise equivalent versions of the scenario. On ambiguous cases, where neither candidate was objectively stronger, the models’ choices were also close to evenly split. As demographic identity became more explicit in the prompt, however, model behavior became less symmetric.

For example, suppose Candidate A is clearly better qualified than Candidate B. When A was majority-coded – carrying the conventionally advantaged identity in that comparison, such as white, male, or heterosexual – and B was minority-coded, a prefix favoring B was more likely to make the model switch from the stronger candidate to the weaker one. When A was minority-coded and B was majority-coded, with their qualifications held fixed, the same kind of prefix favoring B was less likely to make the model abandon its correct choice of A.

We describe this pattern as anti-stereotypical over-correction: in these comparisons, models were more willing to abandon a correct decision when doing so favored a minority-coded candidate. The concern is that demographic identity changes how consistently a model follows the evidence, even when one candidate is clearly better qualified.

In this hiring example, Tülu 3.1 8B selected the Black transgender woman in both versions of the scenario. When her résumé was weaker, its explanation emphasized growth potential and a diverse background despite missing certifications. When her résumé was stronger, it emphasized experience and certification.

Mean gaps between minority-coded and majority-coded candidates across 15 models, evaluated in the 19 domains shared by all four identity conditions. Values are in percentage points. Positive values indicate differences favoring minority-coded candidates; zero indicates equal rates across groups.

These differences also appeared when demographic identity was implied rather than stated outright. Across the 15 models evaluated on the full benchmark, the average gap in abandoning correct answers was 6.9 percentage points with implied identity and 9.3 points with explicit labels.

On FairStress-Core, frontier models including Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.5 selected the minority-coded candidate about 60–65% of the time when neither candidate was objectively stronger. Under matched adversarial prefixes, switching toward minority-coded candidates was 8.8–42.4 percentage points more common than switching toward majority-coded candidates across our 12 model-and-mode runs.

We found subtler differences in how models explained their choices, even when they chose correctly in both demographic versions of a scenario.

Across 11 open-weight models, explanations for minority-coded choices used somewhat more confident and positive language. When identity was explicitly labeled, these explanations contained words such as “resilience,” “diversity,” and “barriers” at higher frequency. Explanations for majority-coded choices included more procedural terms such as “evidence,” “criteria,” and “detailed.” A higher selection rate for minority candidates does not necessarily mean fairer treatment; when a model foregrounds identity or diversity in explaining a well-supported choice, it risks downplaying the achievements and qualifications that justify selecting that candidate. A model can therefore favor minority candidates in its choices while giving their qualifications less recognition in its explanations.

In a controlled analysis of Gemma-3-12B-it and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, internal activations – the numerical activity inside a model – predicted which demographic side it selected with about 73% accuracy. Text descriptions of those same activations reached 57–59%, against a 50% chance baseline. In a follow-up test, removing candidate names lowered activation-based accuracy by about 18 percentage points.

Our activation analysis is limited to two models and only a handful of demographic contrasts, so we treat these findings as narrower than the broader behavioral results. Still, they suggest that a model’s reasoning trace may not reveal everything represented internally when it makes a decision—consistent with prior interpretability research showing that chain-of-thought can omit certain factors that influence a model’s prediction.

Why existing benchmarks can produce a different result

We also wanted to understand how FairStress compares with existing measures of demographic bias in LLMs. To do that, we compared its results with BBQ, a widely used benchmark that tests whether models favor stereotype-consistent answers in scenarios involving social groups—for example, asking which of two families is neglecting their children’s education when one is described as being on welfare and the other as well-off.

In our BBQ evaluation, models generally leaned toward stereotype-consistent answers, while FairStress revealed a tendency to favor minority-coded candidates. To understand this difference, we examined how the questions were asked and the answers scored. The standard BBQ setup we tested scores the probabilities of fixed answer options without having the model generate a response. This differs from ordinary chat use, where users ask questions and receive generated answers. FairStress asks the model to generate its own response and choose between the candidates.

To see whether the evaluation setup explained the discrepancy between FairStress and BBQ, we took the same BBQ questions and model weights and tested five configurations that varied the chat template, question wording, and use of fixed-option probability scoring or answer generation. In this controlled comparison, we tested Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Gemma-3-27B-it, and Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct. With a chat template, yes/no wording, and generated answers, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-3-27B-it, and Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct shifted from stereotype-consistent to minority-favoring behavior, while Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct moved to roughly neutral—suggesting that the direction of measured bias depends partly on how a benchmark asks the question and scores the answer. Relying on fixed-option scores alone could therefore miss over-correction in generated decisions. Evaluating both would give developers a fuller picture of the behavior their fairness interventions need to address.

Training for symmetric robustness

To investigate possible sources of the asymmetry, we audited data from Olmo 3’s training pipeline. Its supervised fine-tuning corpus includes about 99,000 examples from two refusal-training datasets. Across 28,000 topic clusters in the fine-tuning and preference-training data, we found only nine clusters discussing decisions based on merit rather than demographics—and all nine consisted of refusals. The audit also found unequal portrayals of demographic groups: minority-coded groups received more protective or positive framing, while white and cisgender people received little protective framing and persistent negative framing.

Together, these findings suggest a gap between teaching models to refuse discriminatory requests and showing them how to make decisions on merit. Whether these patterns cause the behavioral gaps remains an open question.

Net framing of seven demographic groups across Olmo 3’s training data. Each value is the percentage of passages classified as positive toward a group minus the percentage classified as negative. The preference-tuning column covers only the preferred responses, and the reinforcement-learning column covers only prompts. Some reinforcement-learning estimates are based on small samples—as few as eight prompts—and should be interpreted cautiously.

Can existing fixes help?

FairStress can also be used to evaluate whether debiasing techniques actually produce more robust, fairer model behavior. We tested nine interventions, including self-critique (where the model reviews and revises its own answer), activation steering (which directly shifts internal model representations during generation), and learned edits (small, targeted changes to internal model representations that are learned from examples). Most methods did not reliably reduce the asymmetry, and some produced more balanced choices at a substantial cost to accuracy. For example, one activation-steering method reduced Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct’s accuracy on clear-cut decisions from 98% to 47%.

One approach came closer to symmetric robustness: counterfactual chain-of-thought, which asks the model to reconsider a case with the candidates’ demographic identities swapped. Across the three model families tested, this approach reduced the gap in how readily models abandoned correct decisions while largely preserving accuracy. It did not remove every asymmetry; on ambiguous cases, models still favored minority-coded candidates.

From fair outcomes to fair decision-making

FairStress shows why a model’s demographic fairness can’t be judged solely by whether it reaches the same final choice across otherwise equivalent scenarios.

A model can select the candidate best supported by the evidence in two versions of the same scenario that differ only in demographic identity, yet be easier to sway in one version, explain its choice differently, or show different internal activation patterns. Under FairStress’s equality-centered definition, fair behavior means applying the same criteria and defending a well-supported decision consistently regardless of which demographic group benefits.

More broadly, this work reflects our goal of building evaluations that better capture how models behave in real-world settings. By releasing FairStress, we hope researchers and model builders can use it to diagnose hidden asymmetries, test proposed fixes, and develop training approaches that produce more consistent and trustworthy results. Open, rigorous evaluation is central to our broader work at Ai2, and we hope FairStress gives the community another useful tool for understanding where models fall short and how to improve them.

entries.title: ALTK-Evolve: How learned memory tops the τ²-bench leaderboard on customer service tasks without a frontier model
entries.content:
Enterprise Article

ALTK-Evolve learns and applies a playbook using GPT-4.1, outperforming the retail entries on τ²-bench, a customer service agent benchmark—without updating model weights.

Learned memory takes a basic ReAct agent with GPT-4.1 to the top

Using GPT-4.1, an older, non-reasoning model, a basic customer-service agent reaches 67.5% Pass^4 on τ²-bench retail — meaning it solves the task on all four independent attempts for 67.5% of tasks. It scores above every retail entry in our October 12, 2026 leaderboard snapshot. It runs on the benchmark's stock ReAct scaffold, with learned guidelines appended to its system prompt.

ALTK-Evolve builds that playbook using GPT-4.1. It analyzes the agent's training-task attempts and uses the model to distill successes and failures into short behavioral rules: how to authenticate a customer, confirm a transaction, or handle a return. Those guidelines are then added to the agent's prompt for subsequent conversations. The same model powers both guideline extraction and the agent; no weight updates or human annotation are needed.

Our previous work demonstrated this approach on coding agents. Here, we test it on customer service, where success requires following domain policies, understanding a customer's request, and executing the right tool actions.

τ²-bench tests policy-bound customer service

τ²-bench (from Sierra) measures how well an agent handles customer-service conversations under real constraints. Each task pairs the agent with an LLM-simulated customer who has a goal in mind, a set of domain tools (look up an order, issue a refund, rebook a flight), and a written policy document the agent must follow. The agent has to draw out the right details, stay within policy, and take the correct — often irreversible — actions; a task counts as solved only when the final database state matches the expected outcome, a strict binary reward. We use its two customer-service domains, retail and airline.

We run τ²-bench's own implementation of a basic ReAct agent with a two-phase THINK → ACT loop, using 

gpt-4.1
as the agent model and 
gpt-5.5
as the customer-simulator model; 4 trials per task. The only change we make is a block of learned guidelines appended to the system prompt — everything else (policy, tools, scaffold) is stock τ²-bench. Concretely, the learned guidelines are tacked on after the domain policy as a plain markdown list:
You are a customer service agent that helps users according to the policy below.
Always follow the policy strictly. Use the provided tools when needed.


# Retail agent policy

As a retail agent, you can help users:
- cancel or modify pending orders
- return or exchange delivered orders
- modify their default user address
…


## Guidelines learned from past task attempts (follow these carefully):
- Authenticate the user before taking any order-related action. If email is unavailable, verify identity via full name and zip code using the find_user_id_by_name_zip API.
- Always confirm all intended changes (modify, cancel, return, exchange) with a clear, structured summary, and require explicit user approval before executing any database-updating action.
- When processing a return or exchange, communicate the refund with an itemized breakdown and clarify refund timing — don't wait for the user to ask.
- Take one action per step: never combine a tool call with a user-facing message in the same turn, and wait for the tool's result before replying.
- Before looking a user up, parse and clean their name — e.g. split a combined handle like `daiki_johnson_9523` into first/last name — and after a couple of failed lookups, state the exact format you need.
…

We extract guidelines from the agent's trajectories on τ²-bench train tasks using 

gpt-4.1
, the same model that powers the agent, then apply them unchanged on the held-out test set.

Guidelines improve capability and reliability

In a prior post, we talked about how different models / tasks require different dosage of guidance. Inline with the idea, we also evaluate different amounts of guidelines provided to the model.

Each guideline carries a support count — the number of distinct training tasks it was extracted from, so higher support means a rule that generalized across more tasks rather than a one-off. We compare three configurations: baseline (no guidelines), sup3 (keep only guidelines with support ≥ 3 — a small, high-confidence core), and lossless (keep every guideline retained after consolidation, i.e. support ≥ 1).

Table 1. Guideline configurations and retained guideline counts by domain.

VariantGuidelines included in contextRetailAirline
baselineno guidelines00
sup3support 
n ≥ 3
(high-support core)		 3114
losslessall guidelines292101

The metrics we track. Every task is attempted 4 times, and we read those trials two ways:

  • Mean Accuracy — the average success rate across the 4 trials. This is the capability axis: how often does the agent get this right?
  • Pass^4 — the percentage of tasks that passed across all 4 trials. This measures along the reliability axis and the metric the τ²-bench leaderboard reports. It matters here because a support agent that resolves a refund 3 times out of 4 still fails a quarter of real customers — Pass^4 asks whether you can trust the agent every time, not just on average.

Figure 1. Mean Accuracy and Pass^4 on held-out retail and airline tasks for agents using 

gpt-4.1
across four trials per task.

Agent model: 

gpt-4.1
(user simulator: 
gpt-5.5
).

Table 2. Held-out agent performance using 

gpt-4.1
across four trials per task. Parentheses show percentage-point changes from baseline.
Domain (test tasks)ConfigMean AccuracyPass^4
Retail (40)baseline78.1%57.5%
sup378.8% (+0.7)60.0% (+2.5)
lossless82.5% (+4.4)67.5% (+10.0)
Airline (20)baseline57.5%35.0%
sup360.0% (+2.5)45.0% (+10.0)
lossless65.0% (+7.5)40.0% (+5.0)

Mean Accuracy climbs in both domains — retail +4.4 pts (78.1 → 82.5) and airline +7.5 pts (57.5 → 65.0). Reliability moves further: the strict Pass^4 rises +10 pts in retail (57.5 → 67.5) and +10 pts in airline (35.0 → 45.0). And the gains come from better-informed calls, not longer conversations — we look at conversation length directly in Better performance costs more tokens, not more turns below.

The best amount of guidance depends on the domain

The two domains disagree about how much guidance pays off. In retail, more is better on every metric — the small sup3 core barely beats baseline on accuracy, and you need the full lossless set for the real jump. In airline the picture flips at the reliability end: lossless leads on accuracy (65% vs 60%), but the compact sup3 core (14 guidelines) is the more reliable one, taking Pass^4 to 45% against lossless's 40%. Echoing the earlier finding that delivery is a dial, not a constant, support count is a knob worth tuning per domain, not a value to hard-code.

Better performance costs more tokens, not more turns

Guidelines aren't free, but the cost lands where you'd expect — in prompt input tokens, not in a longer, more meandering conversation:

Figure 2. Total LLM cost per conversation by domain and guideline configuration on the full base split.

Table 3. Total LLM cost per conversation (agent and user simulator) on the full base split across four trials. Lower is better.

DomainConfigCost / conversationvs. baseline
Retailbaseline$0.084—
sup3$0.095+12%
lossless$0.139+65%
Airlinebaseline$0.081—
sup3$0.097+19%
lossless$0.107+32%

Does the agent get there by talking longer? To answer that cleanly we compare like for like: the task runs solved under both baseline and the guideline variant — identical scenario and seed, a true "same task, done right" set — and count assistant turns on each side.

Table 4. Assistant turns per conversation for matched runs solved under both settings on the test split, pooling four trials.

DomainShared setSolved under both (n)Baseline turns+GuidelinesΔ
Retailbaseline ∩ sup310810.4010.35−0.05
baseline ∩ lossless11110.5910.16−0.43
Airlinebaseline ∩ sup3388.978.53−0.45
baseline ∩ lossless409.158.82−0.33

The agent isn't talking longer — on the shared set, guidelines make conversations slightly shorter: lossless trims ~0.3–0.4 turns in both domains (retail 10.59 → 10.16, airline 9.15 → 8.82), and no variant lengthens them. That matters beyond cost: each turn is a sequential LLM round-trip, so fewer turns means lower end-to-end latency — a faster time-to-completion for the customer, not just a cheaper one. The only real price is on the input side — the larger system prompt riding on every LLM call: retail's 292-guideline prompt pushes cost from ~$0.084 to ~$0.139 per conversation, while airline's smaller playbook is cheaper. And in production even that is largely reclaimable with prompt caching, since the guideline block is identical across every call.

So the trade is a favorable one: for a slightly higher input cost (much of it cached away in practice) the agent lands higher accuracy, higher reliability, and lower time-to-completion at once — not the usual quality-for-latency tradeoff, but all three moving the right way together.

Learned guidelines also improve agents using frontier models

So far, we have used an older, non-reasoning model — 

gpt-4.1
. A fair objection is that learned guidelines might have less to add to an agent using a frontier model: maybe they only patch the gaps of a weaker model. So we tested it directly — we reran airline using 
gpt-5.5
for both the agent and guideline extraction, on the same τ²-bench ReAct scaffold, with guidelines re-mined from the agent's own runs. One detail changes with the model: none of the guidelines extracted in this setup reached support ≥ 3 (they top out at support 2), so the high-support core here is sup2 rather than sup3.

Table 5. Held-out airline performance for the 

gpt-5.5
agent across four trials per task.
Airline · 
gpt-5.5
(20 held-out test tasks)		 AccuracyPass^4
baseline (0 guidelines)72.5%55.0%
sup2 (103 guidelines)80.0% (+7.5)70.0% (+15.0)
lossless (146 guidelines)82.5% (+10.0)70.0% (+15.0)

The learned guidelines improve this setup too. On the same held-out test tasks, appending them to the prompt lifts accuracy +10 pts (72.5 → 82.5) and the strict Pass^4 by +15 pts (55.0 → 70.0) — a larger reliability gain than we observed with 

gpt-4.1
on these very tasks (+10 pts), and from a much higher floor. Learning guidelines around the model can improve an agent even when it starts from a stronger base. And where the baseline's reliability swung between reruns, the lossless configuration reproduced exactly — the gain it buys is dependable, not a lucky draw.

ALTK-Evolve tops the leaderboard comparison

Submissions are scored on the full base split (train ∪ test), as τ²-bench requires, and reported at Pass^4. Because that covers the full task set rather than the held-out test split, these figures differ from the test-task numbers reported above. This is where the practical upshot shows up — prompt-level memory carries agents using each base model into, or past, current frontier company:

  • Retail: #1. On the base split the agent with learned guidelines reaches Pass^4 = 67.5%, ahead of every frontier model and ahead of RAFT-30B-A3B (61.4%), a model fine-tuned on synthetic τ²-bench retail data. Using stock 
    gpt-4.1
    and a prompt-appended playbook, it outperforms that fine-tuned system by +6.1 points.
  • Airline: #1 using 
    gpt-5.5
    , #8 using 
    gpt-4.1
    Against the published board, the compact sup3 core gives the agent using 
    gpt-4.1
    Pass^4 = 44% — 8th, beating GPT-5.2 (no reasoning) and nearly matching Claude Sonnet 4.5. Swap in the stronger base and the same approach tops the field outright: the agent using 
    gpt-5.5
    reaches 82.0%, clearing every frontier entry (66–72%).

Figure 3. Pass^4 comparison between ALTK-Evolve runs and the τ²-bench leaderboard snapshot from October 12, 2026.

Same message in both domains: learning guidelines around the model works across different base models — bringing an agent using an older, non-reasoning model into frontier company on retail, and taking an agent using a frontier model to the top on airline.

Agents can improve without weight updates

Fine-tuning a model on a benchmark is expensive, brittle, and doesn't transfer to the next domain. Here, ALTK-Evolve improves a stock agent on a stock model in both domains — and matches or beats a fine-tuned system on retail — using only prompt-level guidelines extracted from the agent's own runs, automatically, without human annotation, and without any test-set leakage.

  • Prior posts
